item.content:encoded:
i should also point out, this probably isn't actually the same guy as in 982.

a common origin, sure. Same accent, same peculiar smell that isn't quite like anything you expect from humans (that's why the secretary described him as 'unwashed'), same association with weird shit. But I don't see Mr Night as being the sort who'd either invent something and go to a patent attorney with it, or arrange the whole thing as an elaborate deception to cover a murder.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Ah, thanks author!

With that in mind, I've stripped away one of the references to him being Polish, and focused more on the disheveled description. He's still called Polish because that's the UIU's best guess based on the evidence, which is mostly heresay from somebody who assumed the accent was Polish.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: For the record, he's probably not actually Polish.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
No one will notice if there is no one around to notice.

In all seriousness, I feel that this is a UIU document that actually gives the UIU some of the FBI flavor the more fantasy/sci-fi delves the GoI take lack. Additionally, placing them against a Chicago Spirit super-cleaner makes for a compelling antagonist.

I'd say others interested in UIU GoI formats should take note, for this is certainly a good way to keep things grounded.

+1.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's a lot to love here. The presentation of Night as a nigh-unstoppable force of death is fitting, and it's good to see SCP-982 formally tied to the growing Spirit mythos.

That said, it's the Pillston death that really sells this one for me. It gives Night some added characterization and keeps the piece grounded. Spooky murders are not uncommon in the SCP universe, but Pillston's demise is a nice reminder that we're dealing with the anomalous mob here.
